title: Board vision without the board

D0.outcome: Explains why a position can be held in mind as a list of pieces and the squares they attack, and gives one task that exercises it.

D1.outcome: With the board hidden, names the colour of a given square, the squares a knight on it reaches in one and two moves, and the squares on a named diagonal.

D2.outcome: From a piece list and three moves in notation with no board, says where each piece stands and which of them is attacked at the end.

D3.outcome: Holds a six-ply line containing a capture, a check and a pawn move, then answers questions about the final position (what is attacked; the legal replies to the check) with no board.

D4.outcome: Over ten games, states the resulting position after his intended move and the likely reply before playing for chosen moves, and is right on the attacked pieces in at least 8 of 10 checks.

misconceptions: Visualising means seeing a picture of the board; it works better as tracking pieces and attacked squares.
Distance in knight moves is easy to count (a knight needs six moves between opposite corners, five is a common slip).
sources: docs/chesscademy-research.md (Visualizing Pieces lesson title, per MAP1 §2 S2)
conditions: Works while the line is short and the learner re-anchors on attacked pieces after each move; error grows with ply count and with captures.
Needs reliable square colours and knight geometry first.
condition_sources: ours; EML §5 item 3 shows even masters slip on knight counts
contrasts: Counting a knight's distance between opposite corners as five instead of six.
Following a line correctly until the first capture, then forgetting which piece was removed.
A sighted calculation with a board on the table does not test this.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PIECE.KNIGHT.D1: knight routes are the usual first visualisation drill
